citation: Hughes, Emily (2023). Meaninglessness and monotony in pandemic boredom. Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11097-023-09888-0. Accepted 13 January 2023; Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) licence.
discipline: philosophy (phenomenology, philosophy of emotion) applied to first-person Covid-19 survey reports
thesis: Using Heidegger's FCM as a vantage point, Hughes first asks whether pandemic boredom is a situative confrontation with relative meaninglessness that sustains everyday absorption, or an existential confrontation with absolute meaninglessness that forces the question of existence; she then argues (her more critical aim) that pandemic boredom makes this distinction difficult to sustain, exposing and exceeding the methodological limitations of Heidegger's interpretation of boredom's ontological structure and of its capacity to discriminate the relative significance of heterogeneous concrete experiences of boredom.

sections.title: §1 Introduction
sections.summary: States both aims (expository phenomenological interpretation; critical exposure of Heidegger's methodological limits); situates 'pandemic boredom' (Hughes's own stipulated term) within the wider multi-disciplinary boredom-studies field intensified by Covid-19; opens with journalistic framings of pandemic time-collapse (O'Connell's 'half-assed end of the world,' Grant's 'boring apocalypse').

sections.title: §2 The philosophy of boredom
sections.summary: Exposits Heidegger's FCM typology of first/second/third-form boredom via Svendsen's situative/existential terminology; develops the co-constitution of attunement (Stimmung) and temporality; traces the historical/epochal reading of boredom as a candidate fundamental attunement of the contemporary technologized age; introduces Heidegger's later, more pessimistic re-reading in the Contributions to Philosophy (Of the Event).

sections.title: §3 A phenomenology of pandemic boredom
sections.summary: Draws on Froese et al.'s 'Experiences of Social Distancing During the Covid-19 Pandemic' survey (~2,543 respondents, Japan/Mexico/UK, June-July 2020); reads open-ended responses to Question 57 ('Have you noticed changes in your experience of time?') through the meaninglessness/monotony frame; introduces Wittmann's 'quarantine paradox' (built on Poppel's time paradox).

sections.title: §4 The significance of pandemic boredom
sections.summary: Argues pandemic boredom is essentially situative (first/second FCM level) and realizes Heidegger's own Contributions-era worry about technologized indifference foreclosing revelatory potential; then argues the situative/existential distinction is destabilized by the pandemic's totalizing disruption of the everyday world itself, and that the relative significance of different people's pandemic boredom cannot be discriminated without attending to heterogeneous social/political/economic conditions; concludes Heidegger's framework needs 'a more critical appropriation.'

constructs.label: profound/deep boredom (FCM 3rd form)
constructs.treatment: existential pole against which pandemic boredom is tested; concluded pandemic boredom does not involve the confrontation with absolute meaninglessness this form requires

constructs.label: being-bored-by (1st form)
constructs.treatment: train-station example; first situative level, directed toward a determinate object/situation that has lost its meaning

constructs.label: being-bored-with (2nd form)
constructs.treatment: dinner-party example; second situative level, more diffuse and pervasive than the first

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: bracketed early as the psychology literature's own frame (outside Hughes's phenomenological method); returns at the close as what Heidegger's account is 'forced back onto' once its ontological distinction destabilizes

constructs.label: boredom proneness
constructs.treatment: noted only as a marker of the wider psychological pandemic-boredom literature (correlation with adherence to social distancing); not adopted as Hughes's own analytic category

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: the paper's two central, ontologically intertwined constructs (attunement and temporality co-constitute each other); read empirically off survey Q57 responses -- meaninglessness as loss of anchoring past/present/future events, monotony as the paradoxical stretch/collapse of time and erosion of chronological structure

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: mapped as an escalating three-form series (dragging time / static now / overwhelming atemporal expanse), re-grounded empirically via Wittmann's quarantine paradox and Poppel's time paradox

constructs.label: boredom-as-regulatory-signal (functional account)
constructs.treatment: not endorsed; addressed only via a footnote distancing Hughes's strictly ontological reading from Elpidorou's drift toward normative/moral/psychological theorizing

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.treatment: Froese et al.'s ~2,543-respondent open-ended qualitative survey ('Experiences of Social Distancing During the Covid-19 Pandemic'); free-text self-report read phenomenologically, not a validated psychometric instrument

readings.claim: Heidegger's FCM stratified typology, read via Svendsen's situative/existential terminology, distinguishes two situative levels (train-station, dinner-party) from one existential level (world-as-whole refusal); situative forms are derived from and grounded in the existential form.
Heidegger speculates that boredom is a candidate fundamental attunement of the contemporary technologized epoch, asking whether Dasein itself has become bored with itself.

By the Contributions to Philosophy (Of the Event), Heidegger grows more hesitant, worrying that calculation, speed and massiveness in homogenized technologized societies may overwhelm boredom's revelatory capacity and produce mere indifference, disillusionment and self-alienation instead.

Pandemic boredom is essentially situative (first/second-level), a confrontation with relative rather than absolute meaninglessness, because what respondents are bored in the face of remains attached to something within the world.

Pandemic boredom realizes Heidegger's own pessimistic Contributions-era worry: technologized, levelled-down societies produce pervasive indifference rather than an existential, revelatory confrontation.

The pandemic destabilizes the situative/existential ontological distinction itself, because it suspends substantial aspects of the familiar world in general (not merely particular contents within an intact world), weakening the assumption that situative boredom cannot be philosophically revelatory.

Heidegger's individualistic conception of boredom has no room for a collective turning-away from the world, since being withdrawn from 'the world' depends on others continuing to be absorbed in it -- a limitation a simultaneous, society-wide pandemic exposes.

Heidegger's train-station/dinner-party examples cannot discriminate the relative philosophical significance of different people's boredom given heterogeneous social, cultural, political and economic conditions; his account is forced back onto psychological state/trait and related dichotomies.

Heidegger's framework remains valuable for organizing pandemic boredom under meaninglessness/monotony, but the phenomenon demonstrates the need for a more critical appropriation of that framework rather than its straightforward application.

interlocutors.name: Heidegger, Martin -- Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics
interlocutors.role: primary phenomenological source for the three-form typology and the historical/epochal reading

interlocutors.name: Heidegger, Martin -- Contributions to Philosophy (Of the Event)
interlocutors.role: later, more pessimistic self-revision Hughes uses to read pandemic boredom as indifference rather than revelation

interlocutors.name: Svendsen, Lars
interlocutors.role: source of the situative/existential terminology Hughes adopts to organize FCM's typology

interlocutors.name: Elpidorou, Andreas (& Freeman, Lauren)
interlocutors.role: contrasted interlocutor: critiqued for moving from Heidegger's ontological framing toward a normative/moral/psychological reading of boredom

interlocutors.name: Froese, Tom et al.
interlocutors.role: authors/leads of the 'Experiences of Social Distancing During the Covid-19 Pandemic' survey supplying Hughes's empirical data

interlocutors.name: Wittmann, Marc
interlocutors.role: cognitive-science complement: 'quarantine paradox' account of pandemic time perception

interlocutors.name: Poppel, Ernst
interlocutors.role: source of the underlying prospective/retrospective time paradox Wittmann adapts

interlocutors.name: O'Brien, Wendell; Chruszczewski, M. H.
interlocutors.role: cited in a footnote surveying alternative boredom typologies (heterogeneous vs. stratified accounts)

tensions.axis: situative boredom (relative meaninglessness, world-directed) vs. existential/profound boredom (absolute meaninglessness, world-as-whole)
tensions.note: Hughes's central diagnostic distinction, adopted from Svendsen's reading of FCM; the paper's critical payload is showing this distinction destabilized, not resolving it in either direction.

Hughes argues pandemic boredom is primarily environment/situation-caused (absence of world-sustaining intersubjective projects) yet its residual significance is agent/situation-relative (heterogeneous factical circumstances), not reducible to a uniform environmental mechanism -- a hybrid position on this axis, not a pure endorsement of either pole.

tensions.axis: Heidegger's strict ontological framing of boredom vs. Elpidorou's normative/moral/psychological (regulatory) framing
tensions.note: Hughes treats Elpidorou's drift toward normative/psychological theorizing as a departure from Heidegger's own project rather than a legitimate development of it.

tensions.axis: boredom as individually structured (Heidegger's examples) vs. boredom as collectively/simultaneously induced (pandemic social distancing)
tensions.note: Heidegger's account presupposes that being-withdrawn from the world depends on others remaining absorbed in it; a society-wide, simultaneous withdrawal has no place in his individualist framework.
